chapter: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
title: Tin Pan Alley numbers and Abbie Mitchell's daily walk-outs
summary: The show's music was by white Tin Pan Alley writers, and Wooding plays the 'Mississippi Mammy' intro whenever Mitchell threatens not to go on.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Uh hunh. Was the music all original, written for that show, or was it other music.
Do you remember any of it?

I can't think of it -- we had a couple of white men, white writers, see? From Tin Pan Alley, they did the show. The only thing I can remember the tune now, I can remember "I Miss My Mississippi Mammy", that's the song we used to open with.
Do you remember how that goes?

Mmm, no I don't think I remember that now. It's got a -- I've even played the thing, you know, but I remember the name of it.

And we had a kid in there too that never amounted to anything later on. Louis Simms. He used to do a dance in it.

But, Abby Mitchell was just like Mistinguette or some of those European stars. Every show, she was quitting.

"Mr. Lyons, I will not go on. I will not do it." "Such and such thing has happened and I'm not going on." And Arthur would look at me and say, "Okay, Sam, hit the introduction."

(laugh)
And we just started the introduction and, let's see if I can think of that. (plays piano), (sings), "I miss my Mississippi mammy --", something like that, anyhow.
We'd do that, and she'd start in singing. Cause she had to come on first, you know.

And then everybody would fall in there afterwards, see. And after you'd listened to what she had said, "Okay Sam, let it go." (laugh) And we'd know that she was coming every day and find some fault with something.
"I won't go on, Mr. Lyons. I will not do it." And, "Okay, Sam, let it go."
